title: RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction

images.desc:
I Introduction



Vehicle trajectory prediction plays an important role in autonomous driving, transportation safety analysis, traffic operations, etc. Despite the development of deep learning models, the vehicle trajectory prediction task is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios.


During the last decade, the fast development of deep learning models provide a chance to predict trajectories by a data driven approach. Models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long-short Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) can interpret individual trajectories as a time series to predict future trajectories. To better consider the interactions between vehicles, multiple approaches are designed to model the interactions among vehicles. Social LSTM is one of the early successful work predicting vehicle/pedestrian trajectories. With the development of the Graph Neural Network (GNN), many studies are using GNN to further model the interactions among vehicles. Recently, models are shifting to the Transformer architecture to replace traditional RNN/LSTM for both the encoder and decoder processes for better modeling capabilities.


Although developments have made, there are still several directions to improve. First, considering the complexity of decision-making process, multiple intentions, or multi-modal capabilities, should be available at the same time. Since different drivers can have different objectives and actions under the same scenario, the problem is better classified as a probabilistic problem rather than deterministic. Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Variational Autoencoders (VAE) are widely used for generating multiple predictions.


Some other aspects of solving the prediction problem are also important. First, the interoperability of previous Transformer-based models are less discussed compared to the model architecture design. Second, it is hard to guide Transformer-based model to learn multi-modal trajectories without manual intention labels (e.g., ’turn left’).


Figure 1 illustrates the basic idea of the proposed prediction process. To provide an intuitive summary before the technical details, Figure 1 illustrates the basic idea of the proposed prediction process. After encoding the historical trajectories, the decoder track generates KK trajectories corresponding to KK modes/intentions. Another decoder generates probabilities for each mode considering spatiotemporal interactions among vehicles. The final outputs are gathered by selecting the trajectory with the highest probability.


Figure 1: Different from most traditional methods, we divide the trajectory prediction process into three steps with two parallel tracks. The first track generates KK trajectories corresponding to KK modes/intentions, the second track generates probabilities for each mode considering spatiotemporal interactions among vehicles as well as considering the inter-modal attentions to rank generated paths/trajectories and give probabilities for each path.


In this study, we designed a Transformer-based, multi-modal trajectory prediction model with the following contributions:


• 

We propose a new spatial attention module considering inter-vehicle motions and dynamics to encode inter-vehicle interactions.



• 

We summarize a “propose then select” strategy to generate label-free multi-modal trajectories efficiently. We hypothesize that agents can have many potential trajectories under similar contexts. The surrounding vehicles only have an impact on the probability of each trajectory.



• 

We design a trajectory ranker by applying an intermodal attention module to “rank” trajectories by predicting the probabilities of each trajectory among KK candidates.



• 

We interpret vehicle decisions by analyzing attention weights between vehicles.

III Methodology



Figure 2: An Overview of the proposed model framework with one trajectory encoder and two parallel decoders.



III-A Problem Definition



Given time tt, the motion state of a vehicle ii is described by a tuple sit=(cit,vit,ait,θit,yit)s_{i}^{t}=(c_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},\theta_{i}^{t},y_{i}^{t}), where citc_{i}^{t}, vitv_{i}^{t}, aita_{i}^{t} and yity_{i}^{t} respectively denote coordinates, velocity, acceleration, angle, and yaw. Thus, given historical time period {1,…,Th​i​s​t}\{1,\ldots,T_{hist}\}, the history trajectories are represented as a series of coordinates:






𝐗={ci1:Th​i​s​t,i∈[1,N]}\mathbf{X}=\{c_{i}^{1:T_{hist}},i\in[1,N]\}

(1)




To predict the future trajectory during the next Tp​r​e​dT_{pred} timestamps from (Th​i​s​t+1)(T_{hist}+1) to (Th​i​s​t+Tp​r​e​d)(T_{hist}+T_{pred}), the future trajectories are represented as:






𝐘={ciTh​i​s​t+1:Th​i​s​t+Tp​r​e​d,i∈[1,N]}\mathbf{Y}=\{c_{i}^{T_{hist}+1:T_{hist}+T_{pred}},i\in[1,N]\}

(2)




In practice, only the future coordinates are of interest since velocities and accelerations are derivable from coordinates. Similarly, for multi-modal prediction, there are k∈{1,…,K}k\in{\{1,\ldots,K\}} possible different modal trajectories represented as follows:






𝐘^i,k={ci,kTh​i​s​t+1:Th​i​s​t+Tp​r​e​d,k∈[1,K]}\mathbf{\hat{Y}}_{i,k}=\{c_{i,k}^{T_{hist}+1:T_{hist}+T_{pred}},k\in[1,K]\}

(3)




where each ci,kc_{i,k} is the kk th mode of estimated trajectory for agent ii. For each kk th mode, there is a probability pi,kp_{i,k} to denote the likelihood of choosing the kk th mode for agent ii. The summation of all probabilities for each agent should equal to 1.






∑k=1Kpi,k=1,∀i∈{1,…,N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{i,k}=1,\;\;\forall i\in{\{1,\ldots,N\}}

(4)




At inference time, among all KK predicted trajectories, the trajectory 𝐘^i,w\mathbf{\hat{Y}}_{i,w} with the highest predicted likelihood pi,wp_{i,w} is used as the final prediction:




w=arg⁡maxk⁡pi,k,i∈{1,…,N}.w=\arg\max_{k}p_{i,k},\quad i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}.

(5)


During training, we supervise the multi-modal decoder with a hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) assignment regularized by ε\varepsilon-greedy exploration: each agent’s modes are usually matched to ground truth through the lowest-error candidate, but a convex mixture with uniform random assignment ensures every proposal track receives supervision early in training; the detailed loss is given in Subsection “Objective function & model evaluation”.




III-B Overall Structure



Figure 2 gives an overview of the proposed architecture of the Rankformer. The architecture is composed of one trajectory encoder and two parallel decoders. The trajectory encoder is used to encode the historical trajectories and the two decoders are used to generate the predicted trajectories and probabilities, respectively. There are different similar Transformer blocks devised to apply attention mechanism over different dimensions of the data. For example, the temporal attention module communicates information among different time frames for each agent. Similarly, spatial attention module communicates information among different agents, especially for agents in close proximity. Inter-modal attention module communicates information among different modes of trajectories. By observing Figure 2, the interactions between different vehicles are only modeled to gain contexts to evaluate the likelihood of each possible trajectories. A special modal attention module is applied to communicate information among KK modes of trajectories to generate probabilities for each mode.




III-C Positional and Spatial Encoding



For trajectory encoder, temporal information is encoded standard positional encoding:






P​E(t,2​i)\displaystyle PE_{(t,2i)}
=sin⁡(t100002​i/d)\displaystyle=\sin\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)

(6)



P​E(t,2​i+1)\displaystyle PE_{(t,2i+1)}
=cos⁡(t100002​i/d)\displaystyle=\cos\!\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)






where t∈[1,…,Th​i​s​t+Tp​r​e​d]t\in[1,\ldots,T_{hist}+T_{pred}] is anytime during the historical and future time frames. Spatial emcoding is applied by fusing the historical record:






S​E​(𝐗)=MLP​(𝐗)\displaystyle SE(\mathbf{X})=\text{MLP}(\mathbf{X})

(7)





For the trajectory decoder, to distinguish between KK trajectories, the encode becomes:






S​E​(𝐗)=MLP​(𝐗)+𝐞intent\displaystyle SE(\mathbf{X})=\text{MLP}(\mathbf{X})+\mathbf{e}_{\text{intent}}

(8)





where 𝐞i​n​t​e​n​t\mathbf{e}_{intent} is a learnable vector for the kk th intention. In summary, the spatial and temporal encoding is computed as:






𝐗o​u​t=SE​(𝐗)+PE​(𝐗)\displaystyle\mathbf{X}_{out}=\text{SE}(\mathbf{X})+\text{PE}(\mathbf{X})

(9)







III-D Temporal Attention Module



Let 𝐗n(l)∈ℝT×d\mathbf{X}_{n}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} be the input feature of one vehicle indexed n∈{1,…,N}n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}. Xn(l)X_{n}^{(l)} is mapped to h-head query 𝐐n(h)\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}_{n}, key 𝐊n(h)\mathbf{K}^{(h)}_{n} and values 𝐕n(h)\mathbf{V}^{(h)}_{n}:






𝐐n(h)=Xn(l)​Wq(h);𝐊n(h)=Xn(l)​Wk(h);𝐕n(h)=Xn(l)​Wv(h);\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}_{n}=X_{n}^{(l)}W_{q}^{(h)};\,\,\,\mathbf{K}^{(h)}_{n}=X_{n}^{(l)}W_{k}^{(h)};\,\,\,\mathbf{V}^{(h)}_{n}=X_{n}^{(l)}W_{v}^{(h)};

(10)




Given key, query and value vectors, a temporal attention mechanism is used to incorporate the dynamics of each vehicle:






headh=softmax​(𝐐n(h)​𝐊n(h)⊤dk)​𝐕n\text{head}_{h}=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}_{n}\mathbf{K}_{n}^{(h)\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)\mathbf{V}_{n}

(11)




Concatenating HH heads, the multihead attention output becomes:






MHA​(𝐗)=Concat​(head1,…,headH)​𝐖O\text{MHA}(\mathbf{X})=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_{1},\dots,\text{head}_{H})\,\mathbf{W}_{O}

(12)




Following the sandwich LayerNorm pattern, the whole attention module becomes:






𝐗nl\displaystyle\mathbf{X}_{n}^{l}
:=𝐗nl+MHA​(LayerNorm​(𝐗n))\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}^{l}_{n}+\text{MHA}\big(\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{X}_{n})\big)

(13)



𝐗n(l+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{X}_{n}^{(l+1)}
=𝐗nl+FFN​(LayerNorm​(𝐗nl))\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}_{n}^{l}+\text{FFN}\big(\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{X}_{n}^{l})\big)






Both encoder and decoder are using the same Temporal Attention Module. However, the decoder module apply the module in parallel for KK times to incorporate KK different intentions.




III-E Spatial Attention Module



Spatial attention module is similar to temporal attention module except the attention network communicate information among vehicles instead of different time frames. Let 𝐗(t)(l)∈ℝN×d\mathbf{X}_{(t)}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} be the input feature of all vehicles at time tt. Then, 𝐐th∈ℝN×d\mathbf{Q}^{{h}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, 𝐊th∈ℝN×d\mathbf{K}^{{h}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, 𝐕th∈ℝN×d\mathbf{V}^{{h}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} be the query, key, and value matrices obtained by projecting the agent features at a given time t∈[1,…,Th​i​s​t+Tp​r​e​d]t\in[1,\ldots,T_{hist}+T_{pred}].






headh=softmax​(𝐐t(h)​𝐊t(h)⊤dk+𝐁(h))​𝐕\text{head}_{h}=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(h)}_{t}\mathbf{K}_{t}^{(h)\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+\mathbf{B}^{(h)}\right)\mathbf{V}

(14)




where 𝐁∈ℝN×N\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} denotes the relative bias matrix to incorporate inter-vehicle motions. Specifically, bi​jb_{ij}, an value in matrix at ii th row and jj th column of 𝐁\mathbf{B}, denotes the relative bias between agent ii and jj, respectively. bi​jb_{ij} is calculated by fusing relative information over a MLP fusing relative difference in historical trajectories:




bi​j=MLP​([Δ​si​j])b_{ij}=\text{MLP}([\Delta{s}_{ij}])

(15)




where Δ​si​j\Delta{s_{ij}} denote the difference between vehicle ii and jj of all motion features (e.g., speed, yaw) defined in si​js_{ij}. Instead of using normalized distance, differentiation is applied to incorporate asymmetrical relationships between two vehicles. In summary, except applying attention network over the vehicles and adding a relational bias term 𝐁\mathbf{B}, all other steps are same as the Temporal Attention Module.




III-F Inter-modal Attention Module



The modal attention module is similar to the temporal attention module, except the attention network communicates information among KK trajectory modes instead of across time frames or vehicles. Before entering the mode probability decoder/predictor, the temporal encoder outputs are pooled over the time dimension to obtain a compact representation for each vehicle and intention mode. Let 𝐙n(l)∈ℝK×d\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} denote the pooled modal features of all KK intention modes for vehicle n∈{1,…,N}n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}, stacked as 𝐙(l)∈ℝN×K×d\mathbf{Z}^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K\times d} across vehicles. Then, 𝐐n(h,m)∈ℝK×dk\mathbf{Q}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{k}}, 𝐊n(h,m)∈ℝK×dk\mathbf{K}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{k}}, and 𝐕n(h,m)∈ℝK×dv\mathbf{V}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{v}} are the query, key, and value matrices obtained by projecting the mode-specific features:






𝐐n(h,m)=𝐙n(l)​Wq(h,m);𝐊n(h,m)=𝐙n(l)​Wk(h,m);𝐕n(h,m)=𝐙n(l)​Wv(h,m);\mathbf{Q}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}=\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{(l)}W_{q}^{(h,\mathrm{m})};\,\mathbf{K}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}=\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{(l)}W_{k}^{(h,\mathrm{m})};\,\mathbf{V}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}=\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{(l)}W_{v}^{(h,\mathrm{m})};

(16)




Given the query, key, and value matrices, a modal attention mechanism is used to incorporate interactions among the KK candidate intentions:






headhm=softmax​(𝐐n(h,m)​𝐊n(h,m)⊤dk+𝐂(h,m))​𝐕n(h,m)\text{head}_{h}^{\mathrm{m}}=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}{\mathbf{K}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+\mathbf{C}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}_{n}

(17)




where 𝐂(h,m)∈ℝK×K\mathbf{C}^{(h,\mathrm{m})}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} denotes a relative bias matrix to incorporate inter-modal relationships. Specifically, ck​lc_{kl}, the entry at the kk-th row and ll-th column of 𝐂(m)\mathbf{C}^{(\mathrm{m})}, denotes the relative bias between intention mode kk and mode ll. ck​lc_{kl} is computed by fusing the learnable intention embeddings through an MLP:






ck​l=MLP​([𝐞k−𝐞l])c_{kl}=\text{MLP}([\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{e}_{l}])

(18)




where 𝐞k\mathbf{e}_{k} and 𝐞l\mathbf{e}_{l} are the learnable intention embeddings introduced in the trajectory decoder (Subsection “Positional and Spatial Encoding”). This bias encourages the model to learn structured relationships among the ordered set of KK modes. In summary, except for applying the attention network over intention modes and adding the relational bias term 𝐂(m)\mathbf{C}^{(\mathrm{m})}, all other steps are the same as in the Temporal Attention Module. The inter-modal attention module is applied only in the trajectory decoder, where KK parallel intention streams are first proposed on pooled encoder features 𝐙n(l)\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{(l)} and then refined through cross-modal interaction before the inter-modal residual summation in the prediction heads.




III-G Path Ranker: Prediction Heads



Following the propose-then-select design in Figure 2,
the trajectory decoder proposes KK candidate futures, while the
Path Ranker scores them using interaction-aware context from the
encoder. Let 𝐇nenc∈ℝT×d\mathbf{H}_{n}^{\mathrm{enc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}
denote the encoder features of agent nn, and let
𝐗^n(−1)∈ℝK×Tpred×d\mathbf{\hat{X}}_{n}^{(-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times T_{\mathrm{pred}}\times d}
denote the mode-conditioned decoder features after the second temporal
attention block (which attends to encoder queries).


Trajectory head.


Candidate trajectories are decoded from the mode-conditioned features:




𝐘^n=MLP​(𝐗^n(−1))∈ℝK×Tpred×2\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{n}=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{\hat{X}}_{n}^{(-1)})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times T_{\mathrm{pred}}\times 2}

(19)





Context branch.


On the Path Ranker side, encoder features first exchange information
across agents and then across time:




𝐂n\displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{n}
=TemporalAttn​(SpatialAttn​(𝐇enc))n.\displaystyle=\mathrm{TemporalAttn}\!\big(\mathrm{SpatialAttn}(\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{enc}})\big)_{n}.

(20)



The resulting context is pooled over time (e.g., last-frame or mean
pooling) to a vector 𝐜¯n∈ℝd\bar{\mathbf{c}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.



Mode fusion and ranking.


Decoder mode features are likewise pooled over the prediction horizon
to 𝐗¯n∈ℝK×d\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}. Context and mode
embeddings are fused along the mode axis by broadcasting context and
adding the learnable intention embeddings 𝐞k\mathbf{e}_{k}:




𝐙n=𝐗¯n+𝟏K​𝐜¯n⊤+𝐄,𝐄=[𝐞1;…;𝐞K],\mathbf{Z}_{n}=\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{n}+\mathbf{1}_{K}\,\bar{\mathbf{c}}_{n}^{\top}+\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{E}=[\mathbf{e}_{1};\ldots;\mathbf{e}_{K}],

(21)


which matches the ⊕\oplus operation in Figure 2
(“modal over modal dimension and add modal embedding vectors”).
An inter-modal attention module then ranks the KK candidates:




𝐙n′=ModalAttn​(𝐙n),\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{\prime}=\mathrm{ModalAttn}(\mathbf{Z}_{n}),

(22)


and mode probabilities follow from a shared scoring head:




P^n=Softmax​(MLP​(𝐙n′))∈ΔK−1.\hat{P}_{n}=\mathrm{Softmax}\!\big(\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{Z}_{n}^{\prime})\big)\in\Delta^{K-1}.

(23)


At inference, the deployed prediction is the maximum-probability mode
𝐘^n,w\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{n,w} with
w=arg⁡maxk⁡{P^n,k}w=\arg\max_{k}\{\hat{P}_{n,k}\}.





III-H Objective function & model evaluation



To train the multi-modal decoder without intention labels, we use a hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) objective with ε\varepsilon-greedy mode assignment. For each agent ii and mode kk, the per-mode error is the mean squared error (MSE) between the predicted trajectory and the ground truth:




di,k=MSE​(𝐘^i,k,𝐘i).d_{i,k}=\mathrm{MSE}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{i,k},\,\mathbf{Y}_{i}\right).

(24)


The hard WTA winner for agent ii is the mode with minimum error,




wi=arg⁡mink∈{1,…,K}⁡di,k,w_{i}=\arg\min_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}d_{i,k},

(25)


and the corresponding one-hot assignment is detached from the computational graph (stop-gradient):




q~i,k=sg​(δk,wi).\tilde{q}_{i,k}=\mathrm{sg}\!\left(\delta_{k,w_{i}}\right).

(26)


Under hard WTA alone, modes that are poor early in training receive no gradient and may collapse before they become competitive. Following the ε\varepsilon-greedy principle in reinforcement learning, we form the final training weights for each agent independently as a convex combination of exploitation (hard WTA) and uniform exploration over all KK proposal modes:




qi,k=(1−ε)​q~i,k+εK,q_{i,k}=(1-\varepsilon)\,\tilde{q}_{i,k}+\frac{\varepsilon}{K},

(27)


where ε∈[0,1]\varepsilon\in[0,1] is an exploration rate annealed to zero over training. This guarantees a minimum supervision mass of ε/K\varepsilon/K on every mode while gradually concentrating learning on the geometric winner. The trajectory regression loss is the qq-weighted sum of per-mode MSEs,




ℒtraj=∑i=1N∑k=1Kqi,k​di,k,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{traj}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{i,k}\,d_{i,k},

(28)


and the mode-probability head πi,k=P^i,k\pi_{i,k}=\hat{P}_{i,k} is trained with soft cross-entropy against the same assignment:




ℒprob=−∑i=1N∑k=1Kqi,k​log⁡πi,k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prob}}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{i,k}\,\log\pi_{i,k}.

(29)


The total training objective is




ℒ=ℒtraj+α⋅ℒprob,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{traj}}+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prob}},

(30)


where α\alpha balances trajectory regression and mode ranking.


For evaluation, we report Average Displacement Error (ADE) and
Final Displacement Error (FDE) in meters. For multi-modal
prediction with KK modes, we report top-1 ADE/FDE using the
highest-probability mode and oracle minADEK\mathrm{minADE}_{K}/
minFDEK\mathrm{minFDE}_{K} by selecting the mode closest to ground truth.




ADE=1N​∑n=1N1T​∑t=1T‖𝐲^n,t−𝐲n,t‖2\mathrm{ADE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{n,t}-\mathbf{y}_{n,t}\bigr\|_{2}

(31)






FDE=1N​∑n=1N‖𝐲^n,T−𝐲n,T‖2\mathrm{FDE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{n,T}-\mathbf{y}_{n,T}\bigr\|_{2}

(32)






minADEK=1N​∑n=1Nmink∈{1,…,K}⁡1T​∑t=1T‖𝐲^n,t(k)−𝐲n,t‖2\mathrm{minADE}_{K}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\min_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{n,t}^{(k)}-\mathbf{y}_{n,t}\bigr\|_{2}

(33)






minFDEK=1N​∑n=1Nmink∈{1,…,K}⁡‖𝐲^n,T(k)−𝐲n,T‖2\mathrm{minFDE}_{K}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\min_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}\bigl\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{n,T}^{(k)}-\mathbf{y}_{n,T}\bigr\|_{2}

(34)

IV-C Model Interpretation



Since there are transformer attention layers to process the interactions between vehicles, it is possible to interpret the model’s behavior by visualizing the “flow” of values within the deep learning model to explore the influence of surrounding vehicles on the vehicle of interest. In practice, just using the attention weights between vehicles is not enough to understand the model’s behavior. Thus, we used a normalized value of the attention weights multiplied by the value of the other vehicle’s embedding vector to visualize the inter-vehicle impacts on trajectories.


Let αi,j\alpha_{i,j} be the attention weight between vehicle ii and vehicle jj. Let 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j} be the embedding vector of vehicle jj. Then, Ii,j=‖αi,j⋅𝐯j‖I_{i,j}=||\alpha_{i,j}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{j}|| represents the magnitude of the “impact” from vehicle jj to vehicle ii. Considering there are JJ vehicles in the scene at time stamp tt, the total impact from all vehicles to vehicle ii at time stamp tt is Ii​(t)=∑j=1JIi,j​(t)I_{i}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}I_{i,j}(t). The normalized impact is Ii​(t)/∑j=1JIi,j​(t)I_{i}(t)/\sum_{j=1}^{J}I_{i,j}(t). In practice, most impacts are from the vehicle itself instead of the surrounding vehicles. Thus, to visualize to impacts, we ignore self impact and only visualize the impacts from other vehicles greater than a threshold (e.g., 0.05).


Figure 3 shows an example scene in local coordinates (gxg_{x}, gyg_{y}). The black and gray lines correspond to the historical and future trajectories, respectively. Blue dots mark each vehicle’s current position. Red arrows connect a vehicle of interest to surrounding vehicles whose embedding values are passed through the attention layer; arrow thickness encodes the normalized impact Ii,jI_{i,j} after discarding self-attention and links below the visualization threshold. Thick arrows therefore indicate strong inter-vehicle influence, while thin arrows indicate weaker but still non-negligible links.


Figure 3: Normalized inter-vehicle impacts (∑‖attention weights×values‖\sum\|\text{attention weights}\times\text{values}\|) in a highway scene for the logits of vehicles. Arrow thickness reflects impact magnitude.


By observing the vehicles, it is clear that the vehicle with cross lane intentions are likely to have higher attention weights to the surrounding vehicles. For example, on the top right corner, vehicle ii is a lane-changing vehicle has a decent attention weight to the vehicle jj on the back in the right lane. This is similar to the patterns of other cross lane change vehicles, which is similar to the real attention patterns of real-world driver’s behavior to focus on the vehicles behind them when changing lanes.
